newsitem.title: USA: Ex-envoy says he wanted to expose corruption.
newsitem.headline: Ex-envoy says he wanted to expose corruption.

text.p: The former head of the private American Institute in Taiwan said on Sunday he was forced from his job when he attempted to bring widespread corruption to light.

"I reported the missing money, the personal profiteering and the sexual harassment to the authorities around and above me," James Wood said in a statement. "But instead of seeing justice served, a quiet cover-up ensued ... I was forced to resign my position."

Wood disputed a Feb. 10 Los Angeles Times article that said Wood sought campaign contributions from Taiwanese by saying Taiwan owed President Bill Clinton money in return for his defence of their security interests.

"I never sought or received any campaign contributions for President Clinton, the Democratic National Committee or anyone else," Wood said. "I never said or implied that Taiwan owed ... Clinton's campaign in return for his protecting their security interests."
Wood headed the American Institute in Taiwan (AIT) until Jan. 17, when he said he was forced to resign.

The State Department, which had no comment on Sunday about Wood's allegations, said AIT is a non-profit corporation established in 1979 to carry out unofficial U.S. relations with Taiwan. Washington has no formal relations with Taiwan.
AIT operates under the policy direction and authority of the secretary of state.
